try hard not think about the trauma

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile is not well aligned with the cognitive formulation. The only active edge is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly arise from the selected appraisals. Overeating and busyness can follow from distressing appraisals, but 'Checking Surroundings' is a threat-monitoring/safety behavior that usually implies an active Threat component or a strong Trigger/Threat linkage, both of which are absent in the formulation and not represented elsewhere in the self-report.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm' is a global current-danger appraisal that typically pairs with a Threat presentation and supports behaviors like environmental scanning. But Threat is not represented as an active component in the formulation, and the rest of the negative appraisals are more about self-doubt and shattered assumptions. This makes the appraisal/strategy pattern clinically incoherent for the specified edge structure.

vignette: Walter had been on his delivery route for nearly two decades, but the evening it changed began like any other Tuesday in November. He was making a stop behind a commercial strip when a man stepped out from behind a metal dumpster, demanded his wallet, and struck him twice across the shoulder and jaw before snatching his gloves and disappearing into the dusk. Walter had come to believe that the world no longer operated by any reliable rules; the assault shattered his long-held conviction that showing up to work and doing the job well would keep him safe. In the days that followed, he found himself certain that if he let his mind rest on what happened, the weight of it would be too much to bear, so he began pushing the memory away before it could surface. The habit of staying constantly occupied took root quickly. Walter threw himself into his work, taking double shifts and volunteering for the longest routes across the county. He refused to sit in the breakroom, preferring to loop back through residential streets and industrial parks just to keep his hands on the wheel. He mapped his route with excessive care, logging extra stops on adjacent blocks just to keep the engine running and the dashboard lights flashing. The van became both his workplace and his refuge, a place where he could keep moving long enough to outrun the stillness that usually brought the November night back to mind. When anxiety tightened his chest in the cab, he reached for the drawer where he kept bags of chips and granola bars, eating steadily not out of hunger but to occupy his mouth and quiet the static in his head. He told himself he was just managing the stress of an older man driving alone, but the eating had become a steady, unconscious ritual. At the same time, he worked hard to keep the memory at bay, repeating delivery sequences under his breath and fixing his eyes on the next turn long before the street sign appeared. He was certain that his mind would fracture if he allowed himself to dwell on the assault, so he treated the memory like a live wire, avoiding it through sheer mental labor. Alongside these routines, a quiet but persistent uncertainty about his own judgment took hold. Walter had come to believe he could no longer trust that he would make the right call. At delivery stops, he would pause at the curb, questioning whether he had locked the cab, whether he had left a tip in the wrong place, whether the customer he passed that morning had noticed his tense posture. The world felt fundamentally unpredictable to him; a sudden shout from a porch or the glare of headlights in his rearview mirror would send his pulse racing, not because he expected another attack, but because his sense of how life should unfold had been stripped away. He avoided certain alleys and loading zones now, not out of fear alone, but because the spaces felt like mirrors of that November night. The daily patterns he had adopted over months had quietly narrowed his days. His wife noticed he stopped talking about his routes, ate dinner too quickly, and sat in the living room with the television at full volume just to keep the silence from creeping in. By spring, Walter's double shifts had worn down his knees, and the constant grazing in the van had changed his weight and his stamina. He found himself hesitating at doorsteps, second-guessing whether he had the right package for the right house, and waking before dawn with his stomach tight. What frightened him most was not the memory itself, but the conviction that letting it in would overwhelm him, so he kept his days packed with driving, eating, and mental rehearsal. His wife had gently suggested he speak to someone, noting how his shoulders stayed drawn up and how his hands refused to rest on the steering wheel without tapping the plastic rim. Walter finally agreed, mostly because the silence at home had become heavy, and because he hoped, if only for a moment, to find a way to trust his own mind again without having to outrun it.
